assessment:
In this study, Baron and colleagues investigate whether pharmacologic activation of integrated stress response (ISR) kinases can prevent pathologic mitochondrial fragmentation associated with disease. The authors address an important gap in therapeutic strategies for neurodegenerative disorders characterized by excessive mitochondrial fragmentation, including Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease Type 2A (CMT2A). While previous work established that the ISR kinase PERK promotes protective mitochondrial elongation during ER stress, and that the GCN2 activator halofuginone induces similar effects, few tools existed to probe whether other ISR kinases could similarly protect mitochondria. The authors therefore screened a nucleoside mimetic library to identify selective activators of alternative ISR kinases.

The key findings demonstrate that two newly identified compounds (0357 and 3610) selectively activate the ISR downstream of the kinase HRI and promote adaptive mitochondrial elongation in an ISR-dependent manner. The authors show that pretreatment with these HRI activators or the GCN2 activator halofuginone prevents calcium-induced mitochondrial fragmentation in MEF cells challenged with ionomycin. Most notably, they demonstrate that pharmacologic ISR activation rescues mitochondrial morphology in patient fibroblasts expressing the disease-associated MFN2D414V variant, restoring mitochondrial length and reducing sphericity to levels comparable to control cells. These effects are consistently reversed by the ISR inhibitor ISRIB, confirming mechanism specificity. The work establishes proof-of-concept that activating different ISR kinases can mitigate pathologic mitochondrial fragmentation induced by both chemical and genetic insults relevant to human disease.

The evidence supporting these conclusions is generally solid, with several methodological strengths. The authors implemented an automated 3D image analysis pipeline that provides objective, quantitative measurements of mitochondrial morphology with large sample sizes (often >1000 mitochondria per condition), substantially improving upon manual classification methods. The screening approach included appropriate validation steps: ISRIB inhibition confirmed ISR-dependence, qPCR verified target gene expression, specificity was tested against other stress pathways, and CRISPRi depletion genetically validated HRI-specific activation. Multiple morphological parameters (bounding box length, ellipsoid principal axis length, sphericity) converge on consistent conclusions. The inclusion of appropriate positive controls (thapsigargin, halofuginone) and the demonstration of effects across multiple compounds strengthen confidence in the findings.

However, several limitations temper the translational implications. Most critically, the patient fibroblasts studied are homozygous for MFN2D414V, while the vast majority of CMT2A cases are heterozygous—a limitation the authors acknowledge but which significantly constrains immediate clinical relevance. The identified compounds exhibit low potency (EC50 >10 μM), limiting their utility as therapeutic leads and necessitating the development of more potent, selective ISR kinase activators. The study focuses exclusively on morphological rescue without assessing whether ISR activation restores other mitochondrial functions disrupted in disease (respiratory chain activity, calcium handling, mitophagy). Additionally, while the ionomycin model provides a controlled system to study calcium-induced fragmentation, it remains unclear whether ISR activation would be protective in more complex in vivo disease models or across the full spectrum of pathogenic MFN2 variants. The work represents an important proof-of-concept with valuable new chemical tools, but substantial additional development is required to establish pharmacologic ISR activation as a viable therapeutic strategy for mitochondrial diseases.
